shows.title: Placeholder Future
shows.description:
Jillian Mayer's fourth solo show with David Castillo turns the gallery into a kind of salvage yard for the future, built largely from materials the Miami artist sourced from a satellite company downsizing as Starlink and its competitors reshape the industry. Glass, aluminum, and other cast-off hardware once destined for orbit become sculptural furniture and objects: a notebook page rendered entirely in fused glass, a chunky aluminum chair that reads like something built for a home off-planet.

Mayer, who has spent over a decade probing how technology reshapes bodies and selves, frames the work less as prediction than as an environment for living inside our attempts to imagine what comes next. A new video, "How to Disappear," uses the tropes of social media tutorials to walk viewers through erasing their own digital footprint, a wry nod to prepper culture and survivalist fantasy. Running through it all is Mayer's own Cuban-American background and her interest in the improvisational repair culture of Cuba's Special Period, when scarcity forced constant reinvention of existing technology.

It's a show about obsolescence and adaptation in equal measure — glossy consumer materials repurposed into something handmade and strange, optimistic and unnerved at once. For anyone who has followed Mayer's decade-plus interrogation of screens, bodies, and the internet, this is a logical and rewarding next chapter.

shows.title: Small Oscillations Among Everyday Forms
shows.description:
Adler Guerrier's fourth solo exhibition at David Castillo is a quiet study of the overlooked corners of Miami's residential landscape — backyards, front yards, stray wildflowers pushing up through stucco, small spiritual offerings left at the foot of a tree. Guerrier, who works as a kind of flâneur through the city's neighborhoods, photographs these marginal scenes and then works them over: transforming images into paper collages layered with rectangular fields of grey, white, black, and olive, or transferring the flora into graphite, acrylic, and gouache drawings that recast the plants in sunset pink and green.

The show's title gets at Guerrier's method directly — the same image of a weed or a wildflower migrates from photograph to collage to painting and back, an oscillation that mirrors how meaning accrues to ordinary things through repetition and attention. A Haitian-born artist long based in Miami, Guerrier has built a body of work around the idea that a neighborhood's demographics, its history of migration and disinvestment, can be read in what grows at its edges.

It's an exhibition that rewards close looking rather than spectacle: modestly scaled collages and works on paper that ask viewers to slow down the way Guerrier does on his walks. For those who know his photography from institutional collections like ICA Miami or the Studio Museum in Harlem, this show extends his ongoing inquiry into landscape, belonging, and the poetics of the everyday into a more intimate, collage-based register.

shows.title: Dissolving Boundaries
shows.description:
German painter Dirk Salz returns to Diana Lowenstein Gallery with a new body of work he calls "multishapes" — an evolution of the reduced geometric vocabulary (square, circle, triangle) he developed in earlier series like "deep dives" and "fadings." Salz builds his paintings less like a traditional painter and more like a sculptor, layering pigment, resin, aluminum, and wood into dense, designed volumes rather than flat compositions.

The title points to the show's central preoccupation: the dissolving line between the tangible and the ethereal, between an object's physical materiality and the shifting light and color effects it produces. By introducing form as an explicit third element alongside his long-standing interests in light and color, Salz pushes his monochromatic fields into a more sculptural, reflective register — surfaces that resist settling into a single, fixed reading no matter how long you look at them.

For longtime followers of Salz's work, this is a show about a artist testing a new formal constraint after years spent exploring the outer limits of color and surface; for newcomers, it's an entry point into a practice that treats painting as an object-making discipline as much as an image-making one.

shows.title: Bakehouse at Forty: Past, Present, Future
shows.description:
Bakehouse Art Complex turns forty this year, and this sprawling anniversary installation treats the milestone as an occasion to think about institutional memory rather than simply celebrate it. The show is split into three curated zones that share the building's old bakery floor: a PAST section assembled by resident artist Philip Lique from archival photographs, brochures, legal documents, and ephemera tracing the building's life from a 1926 Art Deco bread factory to a squatted, artist-reclaimed shell in the mid-1980s; a PRESENT section organized by curatorial manager Krys Ortega that gathers new work from twenty-eight current resident and associate artists, including Beatriz Chachamovits, Adler Guerrier, Amanda Linares, and Sandra Ramos; and a FUTURE section, developed with Michael Maltzan Architecture, that lays out renderings and models for a planned live-work-play campus meant to keep Bakehouse's affordable studios rooted in Wynwood Norte as the surrounding blocks redevelop.

Rather than a conventional retrospective, the installation functions more like an annotated timeline — wall texts, a commissioned soundscape by Archival Feedback built from a century of recorded ambience, and clusters of documentary photography sit alongside actual paintings, sculpture, and design proposals. It rewards visitors who came for a single artist's studio or a mural tour by giving them the larger structure those individual practices sit inside.

For anyone curious how a nonprofit art complex actually works — how a derelict industrial bakery became one of Miami's most important incubators for working artists, and what its next chapter might look like as Miami-Dade real estate pressure intensifies — this is as candid and well-documented an account as the organization has ever mounted of itself.

shows.title: After Icarus
shows.description:
Marielle Plaisir returns to Fredric Snitzer for a solo show built around the myth of Icarus, using the fall as a springboard for pictures that mix historical costume, mythological drama, and a restless, almost baroque layering of pattern and color. Plaisir, a Guadeloupe-born, Miami- and Paris-based painter, has long worked at the intersection of colonial history and personal fantasy, populating her canvases with figures who seem to be assembling and dissolving at once — part portrait, part allegory.

Based on the announcement image, expect large-scale mixed-media paintings that treat the Icarus story less as a cautionary tale about hubris than as a meditation on ambition, flight, and the bodies who take the risk anyway. It's Plaisir's first show at the gallery since her 2023 exhibition "A World of Utopias," and continues Snitzer's long-running commitment to Caribbean and Latin American artists working in figuration.

The show opens with a reception on September 10 and marks the first exhibition of the gallery's fall season after its August closure.

shows.title: Common Skin Fantasy
shows.description:
This two-person show pairs two Miami-based artists in their first exhibition together, built around a psychoanalytic idea from Didier Anzieu about the "skin ego" — the fantasy of boundarylessness between infant and mother before the slow, sometimes painful realization of a separate self. Alicia Bilbao, who works day-to-day as a scientific lab researcher, makes small sculptural figures from epoxy clay, resin, tufts of her own hair, and animal pelts — fragmented bodies and blank-eyed faces suspended in a single uncanny gesture. Alejandra Moros works primarily in paint here, drawing on years of collected reference material — Victorian prosthetics, shedding reptile skin, orchid pollination — to build spectral, half-organic images.

Placed together, the two practices trade the roles of parent and child: Bilbao's sculptures read as brittle, half-formed bodies, while Moros's paintings supply the psychological atmosphere they seem to be dissolving into. Both artists are in their mid-twenties and already carry substantial exhibition histories in Miami and abroad (Moros has shown in Bucharest, Mexico City, and London; Bilbao has had a solo turn at Tunnel Projects), which makes this feel like an early marker for two developing careers rather than a survey.

It's a tightly focused, idea-driven show — good viewing for anyone interested in figuration that leans conceptual rather than illustrative.

shows.title: Crowded Conditions
shows.description:
David Rohn has spent decades turning himself into other people. His long-running (self)-Portraiture project and its offshoot, Street Peeps, found him photographing himself in the likeness of homeless Miamians and pasting the life-size prints onto buildings around the city — a quietly unsettling intervention that treats the city's most overlooked residents with real tenderness. Crowded Conditions marks a turn away from that photographic self-transformation toward painting, and the shift feels earned rather than sudden.

The new paintings are dense, layered things: geometric grids collide with loose, saturated color, and figures drift in and out of legibility against backdrops that nod to Basquiat, Chagall, and Manet without imitating any of them. Rohn has long taught art at Camillus House, the Miami shelter and social-services organization, and it shows — the work has an unpretentious, hard-won quality, more interested in testing what paint can do than in polishing a signature style. Circular and gridded compositions recur throughout, holding the paintings between order and chaos.

What ties the show together is Miami itself, not as backdrop but as subject: a city whose relentless redevelopment has displaced the very people Rohn has spent years photographing and mentoring. Crowded Conditions doesn't resolve that tension so much as sit inside it, which is what makes it worth a visit — a local artist looking hard at his own city's contradictions, in paint that's still finding its footing and all the more interesting for it.

shows.title: Count It All Joy!
shows.description:
Count It All Joy! gathers fifteen Miami-connected artists working across painting, sculpture, textiles, photography, sound, and interactive installation, all circling a single, deceptively simple idea: that joy is worth taking seriously. Curators Donnamarie Baptiste and Arsimmer McCoy frame joy not as an escape from hard times but as a form of resilience — something built, practiced, and shared rather than simply felt.

The roster leans into that range of media rather than a single visual style, with contributors including architect and designer Germane Barnes, photographer Maggie Steber, and painter Dimitry Said Chamy alongside sculptors, textile artists, and sound-based practitioners. That variety suits the premise: joy shows up differently across a photograph, a quilt, a sculpture, or a room-filling installation, and the show seems less interested in tidy consensus than in letting those different registers sit side by side.

Coming from Green Space Miami, a nonprofit platform for Miami-Dade's artists and communities, the show fits a broader pattern in the gallery's programming of foregrounding local voices and collective experience over market-driven spectacle. It's a warm, community-minded exhibition rather than a polished art-fair statement, and worth a visit for anyone curious how a diverse group of working artists answers the same open-ended prompt.

shows.title: Sites of the Self
shows.artist: Diego Gabaldon, Gonzalo Hernández, Sepideh Kalani, Shayla Marshall, Bex McCharen, Lucía Morales, Genesis Moreno, Ana Mosquera, Sheherazade Thénard, Pangea Kali Virga, Nadia Wolff, Ricardo E. Zulueta, José Delgado Zúñiga
shows.description:
Sites of the Self is Oolite Arts' showcase for its current cohort of studio residents, curated by René Morales of the Bakehouse Art Complex. Rather than a single-theme survey, it reads as thirteen distinct investigations of how identity gets built and rebuilt — through family history, queerness, migration, material culture, and the body — brought into conversation across the Lincoln Road galleries.

The curatorial premise leans on Édouard Glissant's idea that selfhood is formed relationally, through encounters with difference rather than in isolation, and the installation follows that logic by moving from intimate, almost confessional works toward pieces staged for public or social space. Expect a wide span of media: painting and works on paper sit alongside sculpture, textile-based pieces (fitting given participant Bex McCharen's tailoring practice), and more research-driven installation work.

Because this is a resident show rather than a themed group exhibition assembled from established artists, it doubles as a status report on who's coming up through Miami's most significant studio-residency program — worth seeing for anyone tracking the city's next generation of working artists as much as for the art itself.

shows.title: From Within
shows.artist: Ana Blanco, Noa Garcia, Emely Yanji, Melina Walsh, TJ Wright
shows.description:
From Within is the debut exhibition of Oolite Arts' inaugural Teen Residency cohort, installed in the gallery's street-facing Vitrine space on Lincoln Road. Five young South Florida artists — Ana Blanco, Noa Garcia, Emely Yanji, Melina Walsh, and TJ Wright — show work made across drawing, painting, sculpture, and mixed media over the course of the residency.

The show reads less like a polished thesis exhibition than a document of first steps: pieces that visibly wrestle with identity, memory, and the artists' immediate environments, made by teenagers just beginning to find a visual language. That rawness is the point — this is a program built to give younger artists their first real gallery context, mentorship, and public audience, and the work on view captures that moment of discovery.

Paired programmatically with the resident show "Sites of the Self" next door, From Within is a quick but worthwhile stop for anyone curious about how Oolite is building a pipeline for Miami's next generation of artists, starting well before the studio-residency level.

shows.title: A Smaller Death
shows.description:
Leo Park's first solo show with Ascaso Gallery gathers a suite of large-scale oil paintings built around the artist's recurring "tattooed bather" motif — nude figures rendered as flattened fields for invented tattoo-like markings drawn from graffiti, runes, petroglyphs, and Hebrew letterforms. The Stockholm-based painter, who trained at Konstfack, works in a loose, cartoon-inflected Neo-Expressionism that visibly digests a whole lineage of modern figuration, from Picasso and Henry Moore to George Condo and Philip Guston, whose oversized, single-focus eyes turn up throughout the canvases.

The paintings on view are the artist's largest and most narratively layered to date, deepening a beach-and-bather iconography he's worked through since 2019. A few pieces lean on specific references worth knowing going in: the title work nods to the French idiom for a moment of release, while "Ikaros Falling into the Sea Behind a Tattooed Woman" quietly restages both Bruegel's drowning Icarus and David Hockney's "A Bigger Splash." None of this is spelled out on the canvas — Park keeps his figures abstracted enough that the stories stay suggestive rather than illustrated.

It's a show that rewards standing close: the tattoo-like textures covering each body are where most of the incident happens, turning otherwise simple, blocky compositions into fields you can keep reading. For anyone tracking how younger painters are metabolizing twentieth-century figuration, this is a clear and confident data point.

shows.title: Wifredo Lam: Around the Galleries
shows.dates_note: Gallery's exhibitions page lists this as a current exhibition spread across the 1st and 2nd floors of the 3155 building; no opening or closing dates are published.
shows.description:
This standing presentation gathers more than twenty works by Wifredo Lam spanning five decades, from an early 1932 portrait through the Afro-Cuban surrealist paintings of the 1950s-70s and on to his late prints and ceramics. It functions less like a single-theme show than a survey of the range of media Lam worked in over his career: oils, mixed-media works on paper, terracotta plates, bronze and brass sculpture, and the celebrated Apostroph'Apocalypse print suite made with poet Gherasim Luca in the 1960s.

Highlights include a large 1955 oil, "Untitled (Arcane Dreams)," alongside smaller ink drawings, pastels, and the artist's recurring "femme cheval" (horse-woman) hybrid figures that fuse human, animal, and Afro-Caribbean spiritual imagery. Several pieces carry exhibition and auction histories reaching back to the 1990s and come with certificates from the Lam estate, underscoring the gallery's decades-long specialization in authenticating and placing the artist's work.

For anyone new to Lam beyond his best-known canvases, this is a chance to see the breadth of his practice in one place — from intimate works on paper to the metal sculptures and prints that are shown far less often than the paintings that made his reputation.

shows.title: Gina Pellón: Centennial (1926-2026)
shows.dates_note: Gallery's exhibitions page lists this as a current show marking the centennial of the artist's birth; no opening or closing dates are published.
shows.description:
Marking one hundred years since Gina Pellón's birth, this show brings together more than twenty paintings, collages and works on paper made between 1970 and 2014, tracing the arc of her career from her Paris years to the final decade of her life. Pellón left Cuba for France after the Revolution and never returned, building a career among the Paris surrealists and the CoBrA group while developing a highly personal, expressionist language built from luminous color and recurring female figures.

The works on view move between abstraction and figuration — faces, women, and gatherings dissolve into fields of raw pigment, described by contemporaries as conveying "the joy of being." Mixed-media canvases like "Mantilla for Silence" and "Memories of Struggles" sit alongside smaller ink drawings and collages, giving a sense of how consistently she returned to the same handful of motifs across four decades in exile.

Pellón spent the final ten years of her life represented by Cernuda Arte, which now holds her archive, and the gallery has drawn on that relationship for a show that doubles as a modest retrospective — useful viewing for anyone curious about the lesser-known women of the Cuban diaspora's postwar generation.

shows.title: Juan Roberto Diago: Selections from 1998-2019
shows.dates_note: Gallery's exhibitions page lists this as a current show spread across the 3143 building; no opening or closing dates are published.
shows.description:
This selection of eleven works traces two decades of Juan Roberto Diago's practice, from raw, collaged canvases made in Havana in the late 1990s to a large found-object installation from 2019. Diago works with discarded and salvaged materials — wood, scrap metal, an actual refrigerator carcass — building surfaces that carry the physical wear of the objects themselves, an approach tied to his long engagement with Afro-Cuban history and the material conditions of everyday life in Cuba.

Works like "Eating Knives" and "The Daily B.S." show his early collage-and-mixed-media paintings, thick with layered black pigment and found scraps of paper, while "Shantytown Los Sitios, Havana" — forty handmade miniature houses built from reclaimed wood — represents the more sculptural, installation-based direction his work has taken since the 2000s. Several pieces here were shown in his 2019 Lowe Art Museum retrospective and in the accompanying Harvard University Press monograph on his work, giving the show some institutional weight beyond the gallery walls.

It's a useful complement to the more decorative Cuban modernism the gallery is known for, showing a contemporary artist working through questions of race, poverty and memory with materials that carry their own history.

shows.title: Tomás Sánchez: A Selection of Artworks from the 1970s to the 2000s
shows.dates_note: Gallery's exhibitions page lists this as a current show; no opening or closing dates are published.
shows.description:
This show surveys four decades of Tomás Sánchez's work, from student-era lithographs made in Havana in the early 1970s to the meditative landscape paintings that made his international reputation. Sánchez trained at Havana's San Alejandro Academy and the Escuela Nacional de Arte before leaving Cuba in 1989; he now lives in Costa Rica, and the tropical forest has remained his defining subject ever since.

The paintings on view — "Shore," "Island," "Low Cloud Seen from the Mountain" — show his hyperreal, almost hallucinatory treatment of jungle, water and sky, dense with vines, moss and sunlight that the artist has described as emerging from meditative states rather than direct observation. Earlier lithographs and works on paper from the 1970s reveal a rougher, more expressionist side of his practice, shaped by his teacher Antonia Eiriz, before landscape became his singular focus.

Several works carry exhibition histories running through Cernuda Arte's own past Sánchez shows dating back to 2010, making this less a single new exhibition than an accumulated presentation of pieces the gallery has placed and re-shown over many years — worth a look for the density of landscape painting alone.

shows.title: Ines Silva: Rhythms of Geometry
shows.description:
Ines Silva trained as an architect, and it shows: this exhibition of Plexiglas reliefs, columns, folding screens and suspended structures is built on mathematical armatures — the golden ratio, the Fibonacci spiral, Le Corbusier's Modulor — that never announce themselves as theory so much as produce a quiet, almost musical sense of balance in the finished pieces.

What comes across most in the work is transparency and movement. Silva's forms are layered and often kinetic, meant to be walked around rather than viewed head-on; light passes through and across the colored planes differently depending on where you stand, so the pieces keep shifting as you move through the gallery. It's geometric abstraction that behaves more like sculpture in flux than fixed object.

For a gallery known largely for Latin American modern and contemporary painting, this is a change of register — a show built entirely around material transparency, structure and the viewer's own movement through space, worth seeing for how differently it rewards a second and third look.

shows.title: In Depth
shows.dates_note: Gallery's current exhibitions page (exposiciones) lists this show under "EN CURSO" (currently on view) at the Miami space, though the show's own page header reads "Abril – Julio, 2026"; exact current dates unconfirmed.
shows.description:
Orestes Hernández's paintings and sculptures resist easy reading by design. Spanning roughly ten years of his output, the works gathered here move freely across chronology rather than tracing a linear development, throwing together large-scale acrylic canvases, smaller studies, and painted wooden sculptures of strange, hybrid creatures that seem to belong to a private mythology.

What holds the show together is Hernández's interest in perceptual slippage — figures that dissolve representation, metaphor and coherence rather than build toward them. Winged beasts, ambiguous bodies and invented characters recur across the paintings, rendered in flat, saturated acrylic that gives them a cartoonish surface concealing more unsettled content underneath. The wooden sculptures, built from assembled and painted forms, extend the same logic into three dimensions.

It's a disorienting, playful body of work that rewards slow looking rather than quick categorization — closer to encountering unfamiliar creatures than to reading a coherent narrative, which seems to be exactly the point.

shows.title: SCAPES: Territories of the Seen and Unseen
shows.dates_note: Gallery's site confirms the opening reception as Friday, September 4, 2026, 5-9pm, but publishes no closing date.
shows.description:
SCAPES gathers a wide range of artists working across generations and media around the idea of landscape — not as a fixed genre of scenery, but as something built from memory, displacement and the act of seeing itself. The exhibition draws loosely on John Berger's writing on vision and landscape, and it shows: works move between recognizable natural and built environments and much more interior, abstracted territory.

The checklist spans resin and acrylic works by Tony Vazquez-Figueroa, glitter-inflected oil paintings by Elisabeth Frieberg, a large watercolor by Alexandre Arrechea, geometric paper works by Karen Rifas, quiet oil landscapes by Tim Buwalda, and a large relief print on Japanese paper by Jennifer Basile — alongside pieces by Cuban modern masters Rafael Soriano and Tomás Sánchez and by Ana Mendieta, whose earth-body works are foundational to any contemporary conversation about land and displacement.

Given how many of the participating artists carry personal histories of exile or migration, the show's interest in "where landscape ends" reads as more than a curatorial conceit — it's a genuine throughline connecting artists who came to the idea of place from very different directions and eras.

shows.title: Sanctuary: Our Sacred Place
shows.description:
Woosler Delisfort, a documentary photographer who grew up in Little Haiti, spent years inside the neighborhood's churches, temples, and mosques to make this series, and the result reads less like reportage than like a long, patient act of listening. More than seventy photographs trace how Miami's Haitian, broader Caribbean, African, and Indigenous communities carve out sacred space — in storefront chapels, backyard ceremonies, and sanctuaries that double as community anchors.

What makes the project distinct is its refusal to treat these spaces as anthropological curiosities. Delisfort shoots as an insider, and the images linger on gesture and light rather than spectacle: hands raised mid-prayer, congregants caught between song and stillness, the worn thresholds of buildings that have held generations of ritual. Curated by Marie Vickles with Carl Juste, the show frames these pictures as evidence that faith infrastructure is also cultural infrastructure — a source of healing, organizing, and continuity for a neighborhood often narrated from the outside.

Showing the work at the Little Haiti Cultural Complex closes a loop for Delisfort, who is exhibiting in the community he documents. It's a homecoming show in the plainest sense, and it's worth seeing before it closes for the intimacy of its access as much as for the sweep of its subject.

shows.title: Off the Shelf
shows.description:
Miguel Ferrando died in 1995 at thirty-eight, and this survey of more than thirty works made over two decades is an overdue chance to see why he mattered. Born in Santo Domingo and raised from age five in New York, Ferrando split his visual imagination between the Lower East Side's queer downtown scene — he performed drag at the Pyramid Club and ran with artists like Darrel Ellis and Malcolm Morley — and the landscapes, saints, and vernacular imagery of the Dominican Republic he kept returning to.

The paintings on view move between portraiture, landscape, and still life, and they wear their art-historical debts openly: Caravaggio's tenebrism, Velázquez's portraiture, the tropical modernism of Caribbean painters who came before him. Rather than settling into any single inherited style, Ferrando fused realism, impressionism, and symbolism into something specific to his own double vision — an artist who was never fully of one place, working images of Catholic saints, dashboard icons, and New York monuments into the same visual language.

The show argues for Ferrando's overlooked place in the history of Dominican diasporic art, alongside artists like Freddy Rodríguez and Tony Capellán with whom he shared thematic ground. It's a rare opportunity to see a body of work that has been largely absent from major exhibitions until a recent wave of reappraisal in New York — and the first time it's been shown at this scale in Miami.

shows.title: Sculptures for Plants and People
shows.description:
Anders Herwald Ruhwald's ceramic sculptures are built to be lived with rather than merely looked at. This presentation of roughly ten hand-formed, large-scale works doubles as vessel, planter, and seat — some pieces hold live plants that will keep growing for the run of the show, others simply invite visitors to sit down inside the installation. The premise is simple and a little radical for a gallery: the work is designed to change while it's on view, and the audience is asked to participate in that change by watering, sitting, and paying attention.

Formally, the sculptures split between two registers. Some are tall, columnar, almost figural — rising from wide bases into crown-like openings that read as heads or receptacles. Others cluster into irregular, vertical growths that feel more geological than architectural. The surfaces throughout are rough and heavily worked, keeping visible the marks of the artist's hands and emphasizing clay's material presence over any glazed polish.

Ruhwald, a Danish sculptor who trained at the Royal College of Art and has taught ceramics at Cranbrook and the School of the Art Institute of Chicago, has spent his career probing the space where domestic objects, bodies, and architecture blur together. Here he adds a living, botanical element — ordinary plants pulled from the local landscape and re-contextualized inside the gallery — turning each sculpture into a slow-motion collaboration between the artist, the plant, and whoever stops to sit with it.

shows.title: Interdum Mane
shows.description:
Laure Mary paints in the hour before most people wake up, and her debut Miami solo show is built entirely around that liminal window. The Paris-based artist begins her days between four and five in the morning, and the dusky, surrealist oil paintings that result — hats standing in for identity and disguise, chairs suggesting absence or hierarchy, houses nested inside houses — all carry the specific unease of the moment before full consciousness arrives.

Mary works squarely in the lineage of Dutch Golden Age painting and Flemish Baroque still life, borrowing that tradition's taste for symbolism and vanitas but recasting it in a contemporary, dreamlike register. Doorways and landscapes recur as thresholds that never quite resolve into legible space, and figures — when they appear — read more as props in a private psychological drama than as portraits. The paintings are small in number but dense with recurring motifs, rewarding the kind of slow looking the artist herself practices at dawn.

Titled after the Latin for "sometimes in the morning," the show is less a suite of individual pictures than a sustained meditation on a single daily ritual, making a convincing case for Mary as a painter who has built a genuinely personal iconography out of the most ordinary hour of the day.

shows.title: Photosynthesis
shows.description:
Jesse Zuo's first exhibition at the gallery is built from small, quiet paintings — most just ten by eight inches — that catch light doing something specific and fleeting: crossing a tabletop, glancing off soap, settling on a friend's gesture mid-motion. The Chinese-born, New York-based painter works in a soft, contemplative realism where color reads as a byproduct of observed light rather than a compositional decision, and the show's title makes the metaphor explicit: light absorbed and slowly converted into paint.

The subjects are aggressively unglamorous by design — a table setting, a bar of soap, an unremarkable interior moment — and that's the point. Zuo isn't hunting for drama in the everyday; she's interested in what sustained attention does to things nobody bothers to look at twice. The result is a body of work that trades spectacle for stillness, asking viewers to slow down to the same pace at which the paintings were made.

As Zuo's first show at Piero Atchugarry, Photosynthesis functions as an introduction to a young figurative painter whose palette has grown steadily softer and more restrained, and whose interest in interiority over incident sets her apart from more overtly narrative peers working in realism today.

shows.title: Acoples (Couplings)
shows.description:
Ernesto Garcia Sanchez builds these new panel paintings only to take them apart. Each piece begins as a resolved composition of hard-edged circles, cylinders and stripes in acrylic and crayon on plywood, then gets physically cut into fragments and reassembled into a new configuration — a process the Cuban, Mexico-based artist calls "coupling." The resulting works sit somewhere between painting, drawing and object, their surfaces bearing the visible seams of where one geometric logic was interrupted and another grafted on.

The show is Sanchez's fourth exhibition with Mindy Solomon and his third solo outing there, following earlier presentations like "Greetings from Yucatán" and "Linearity." His geometric vocabulary — stacked cylinders, checkerboard grids, bands of red, black and warm wood tones — has roots in his training at Havana's San Alejandro Academy and ISA, and in the community art initiatives (including his own Taller 62 project in Mérida) that have run alongside his studio practice for over a decade.

What makes "Couplings" more than an abstraction show is its insistence that a finished painting is only a pause, not an endpoint. By reopening completed compositions to cutting and reconstruction, Sanchez treats resolution itself as provisional — each new "coupling" a fresh argument about how forms, colors and fragments can be renegotiated into different relationships. It's a quietly conceptual proposition delivered through very physical, tactile objects.

shows.title: Falling Tide Can Turn
shows.description:
Brooklyn painter Matt Phillips works directly on canvas without preliminary drawing, building up and scraping back layers of pigment and silica until simple shapes — wedges, bands, wave forms, shallow horizons — settle into place. The paintings in "Falling Tide Can Turn," his third solo show with Mindy Solomon, read as both still and in motion: a curved line can describe a firm edge one moment and an expanding crack the next, and forms that look complete keep implying the possibility of further change.

That instability is the point. Phillips has spoken about wanting a single image to support multiple readings — as a picture of a named, resolved form, or as evidence of an ongoing action like bending, floating or unfurling. The pastel-toned palette and flattened geometry give the work an appealing lightness, but underneath is a fairly rigorous meditation on perception: the idea that nothing pictured is really fixed, and that what looks like loss or dissolution might just be transformation in progress.

It's a good pairing with the show's title, borrowed from Phillips's own writing about the work — a reminder that even a receding tide eventually reverses. The paintings themselves, ranging from intimate 24-by-30-inch canvases to larger 66-by-44-inch works, offer plenty of room to sit with that idea.

shows.title: Electromagnetic Signature
shows.description:
This two-person show pairs a painter and a sculptor who both treat surface as something porous rather than sealed. Kiwha Lee, showing at the gallery for the first time, paints with layered, hand-printed patterns derived from Korean and Chinese resist-printing traditions, building translucent screens on canvas that she likens to the jali — the perforated architectural lattice that filters light and air rather than blocking it outright. The effect is paintings that seem lit from behind, where it's genuinely hard to tell what's surface and what's depth.

Julia Kunin, back for her second Mindy Solomon exhibition after 2023's "Dream Machine," contributes glazed ceramic sculptures that fuse figure, machine and architecture into gender-fluid, sometimes glittering totems — objects that draw on Art Nouveau decorative traditions and a personal vocabulary of feminist and queer symbolism. Her small-scale pieces (an alarm clock, a novelty cube, a "cupping game") read like talismans pulled from an imagined domestic sci-fi.

Placed together, Lee's paintings and Kunin's sculptures share a vocabulary of pattern, reflection and hidden interior structure, and the gallery's framing of the show around "electromagnetic" energy is a fair description of how the two bodies of work seem to charge the room between them — one flat and permeable, the other dense and three-dimensional, both concerned with what passes between visible surface and whatever lies behind it.

shows.title: Always Looking at Palm Trees - A Botanical Conversation
shows.description:
French-Moroccan artist Mehdi-Georges Lahlou makes his Miami debut with a body of work that turns the palm tree — Florida's ultimate tourism cliché — into a vehicle for thinking about migration, colonialism and ecological precarity. Working across sculpture, installation, photography, drawing and printmaking, Lahlou takes the palm's layered history in Miami (native Royal and Cabbage Palms growing alongside imported Coconut Palms brought in to manufacture an image of tropical leisure) as a way into questions about what gets naturalized, displaced and rewritten over time.

The show is loosely structured as a riff on "The Conference of the Birds," the twelfth-century Sufi poem in which birds searching for a legendary creature discover that they themselves are what they sought; Lahlou substitutes a "conference of palms" for the birds, inviting viewers to seek out the trees' meanings rather than take them for granted. Across the installation, his own body appears in vegetal and hybrid forms, archival images of colonial violence are partially obscured by ash, and queer performers animate presences that blur bodily and botanical registers.

It's a conceptually dense show wrapped in an appealingly literal premise, and it marks a first U.S. presentation for an artist better known in Europe — reason enough to catch it before it closes at Voloshyn's Miami space.
